subtype: Approach: mixing practice with fun to stay motivated [Revision]
passage:
"Arnab-sir, can I say something?"
"Go on, Sahil."
"I've done scales every day for a month. I'm... bored. I don't even want to open the keyboard."
"Hmm. I noticed you came late twice."
"Could I learn one film song? The one from the rain scene? I'd still do the scales first."
"Scales first, then the song?"
"Yes. Like dessert. Ten minutes of scales, then ten minutes of the song."
"And if you skip the scales?"
"Then no song that day. My rule."
"All right. I'll write out the melody. But it uses the same C major scale you hate."
"Then I'll hate it less."
Two weeks later, Sahil's mother told Arnab-sir he'd been practising without being told.

qa.q: How long had Sahil been doing scales every day?
qa.a: For a month.

qa.q: How was Sahil feeling about practice before the talk?
qa.a: Bored and unwilling; he didn't even want to open the keyboard. 😴

qa.q: What else could Sahil do if the film song gets boring too?
qa.a: Choose a new reward piece each month with Arnab-sir, so the treat stays fresh while the scales continue.

qa.q: How does Arnab-sir see the request?
qa.a: Arnab-sir takes it seriously, having noticed the lateness, and agrees while tying the song to the same scale.

grounding: A bored boy asks his teacher to add a film song he likes and uses it as a reward after finishing his scales.

subtype: Approach: mixing practice with fun to stay motivated [Revision]
passage: Last year I nearly gave up the tabla. I'm Divyansh. My guru, Vijay-ji, had me doing the same basic strokes for weeks, and practice felt like eating plain rice every day. I started "forgetting" to practise. Then one evening I heard a film song on the neighbour's radio with a tabla part that made my feet tap. I got brave and asked Vijay-ji if I could learn it. Vijay-ji thought for a while and said yes, but only after the exercises. So that became my deal with myself: twenty minutes of strokes, then the film song as a treat. I practised more that month than in the three months before. I still don't love the strokes. But I don't skip them now.

qa.q: What did practice feel like before the change?
qa.a: Like eating plain rice every day.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel asking Vijay-ji about the film song?
qa.a: Divyansh felt nervous and had to get brave before asking.

qa.q: What else could keep practice interesting after this song?
qa.a: Divyansh could ask Vijay-ji for a new favourite piece each month, still earned after the exercises.

qa.q: How might Vijay-ji see the change?
qa.a: Divyansh practised more that month than in the three before, so Vijay-ji is likely pleased the idea worked.

grounding: Looking back, a child bored with basic tabla strokes asks the teacher to add a film song and uses it as a reward after exercises.

subtype: Approach: ignoring the teasing at first [Thinking]
passage: Every day at the water cooler, two boys from 7B called Jomon a name about his accent and knocked his bottle aside. Jomon had a plan. "If I don't react, they'll get bored." So he stared at the wall and filled his bottle slowly. On Monday they said it twice and left. On Tuesday, only once. He thought it was working. On Thursday they followed him to the stairs, saying it louder, and one of them yanked his bag strap. His classmate Charu saw it. "Ignoring isn't stopping them," Charu said. Jomon's jaw was tight. "It worked a bit." "A bit isn't enough. Come on." They went to the class teacher before the next period. She listened to both of them, told Jomon it was not his fault, and walked straight to the 7B teacher's room while they waited.

qa.q: Where did the boys tease Jomon each day?
qa.a: At the water cooler.

qa.q: What did Jomon hope would happen, and how did he feel, as he stared at the wall?
qa.a: He hoped they would get bored if he didn't react; he felt tense but hopeful that staying calm would end it.

qa.q: What else could Jomon do besides ignoring?
qa.a: Tell a teacher early, as he finally did with Charu, because adults can stop teasing that ignoring only slows down.

qa.q: How does Charu see the ignoring plan?
qa.a: Charu thinks 'a bit' isn't enough and pushes Jomon to tell the teacher straight away.

grounding: A boy tries ignoring teasing, which helps a little for a few days, until it grows worse and he goes to a teacher.

subtype: Approach: ignoring the teasing at first [Thinking]
passage: I'm Arnab, and I sit behind Lalit. Since the start of term, a boy in our class has been flicking Lalit's ear in the line and calling him "Specs". Lalit told me his plan was to act as if he couldn't hear. For a week it sort of worked: the boy did it less, maybe got bored. Then on Monday he snatched Lalit's glasses and passed them round the room. Lalit still said nothing. His hands were shaking when he got them back. I don't know what he was feeling, but I knew ignoring had stopped working. At lunch I asked him to come with me to Mrs Pinto. He came. She listened, told him it wasn't his fault, and moved the other boy's seat that afternoon. She also said she would call Lalit's parents that evening.

qa.q: What did the boy do on Monday?
qa.a: He snatched Lalit's glasses and passed them round the room.

qa.q: What might Lalit's shaking hands suggest?
qa.a: He was frightened and upset, even though he stayed silent.

qa.q: What else could Lalit have done when the teasing started?
qa.a: Told a teacher early; ignoring can be a first step, but once it continues an adult needs to step in.

qa.q: How does Arnab see the ignoring plan?
qa.a: Arnab saw it work a little at first, but realised after the glasses that it had stopped working.

grounding: A classmate watches a boy's plan of ignoring teasing work briefly and then fail, and takes him to a teacher.

subtype: Approach: telling a teacher or parent with details [Action]
passage:
Class teacher's note, 12 August.
At break Afreen handed me a folded page from her rough book. She had written, in neat columns: date, what was said, where, and who saw. Three entries in two weeks: names shouted at her across the lunch table, her tiffin tipped over near the tap, and a nasty note passed in class. Beside each were the names of classmates who had been there. She said she wanted me to know exactly, not just "they're mean". I told her she had done the right thing and that none of this was her fault. This afternoon I spoke to the two students she named and to the witnesses, whose accounts matched hers. I have informed both families and the counsellor today, and I will check in with Afreen tomorrow morning.
Kunal, Class 5 teacher

qa.q: How many entries were on Afreen's page?
qa.a: Three entries in two weeks.

qa.q: Why did Afreen write everything down, and how did she seem to feel?
qa.a: She wanted to be taken seriously; she seemed determined, though probably nervous about telling.

qa.q: What else could Afreen do if something happens again?
qa.a: Add it to her record and tell Kunal the same day, so the teacher can act while it is fresh.

qa.q: How did the clear record help Kunal?
qa.a: Kunal could check with the witnesses, whose accounts matched, and act that same afternoon.

grounding: A teacher's note records a girl bringing a written record of what was said, when and who saw, so the teacher could act on clear facts.

subtype: Approach: telling a teacher or parent with details [Action]
passage:
Thursday
Today I finally did it. For two weeks the group at the back bench has been singing a song about my braces every time I pass. Last night I wrote it all in my notebook, the way Dolma's older sister once told her: the date, the exact words, where it happened, and who heard. Dolma heard it four times, Sameer twice. At lunch Dolma came with me to Mrs D'Souza. I gave her the page. My voice wobbled, but the page didn't. She read all of it and said, "Thank you for writing this down. This is not your fault, Aditi." Before the last bell she had talked to the group and to Dolma, and she said she would phone Mummy tonight. She did. Mummy hugged me for a long time.

qa.q: How many times did Dolma hear the song?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel handing the page to Mrs D'Souza?
qa.a: Aditi was nervous, with a wobbling voice, but brave enough to hand it over.

qa.q: What else could Aditi do if the singing starts again?
qa.a: Aditi could add it to the notebook and tell Mrs D'Souza the same day.

qa.q: How did Mrs D'Souza respond?
qa.a: Mrs D'Souza thanked Aditi, said it was not Aditi's fault, spoke to the group and to Dolma that day, and phoned Mummy that night. 🤍

grounding: A diary entry shows a child writing down exactly what was said, when and who heard, and giving it to the class teacher, who acts that day.

subtype: Approach: hitting back in anger [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday: For the third day running, a boy from the next section grabbed Joseph's cap at recess and tossed it onto the canteen roof. Joseph's friend Nazia said, "Tell Sir." Joseph said, "I'll handle it."
Tuesday: When the boy reached for the cap again, Joseph shoved him hard with both hands. The boy fell against a bench and cut his elbow. A teacher saw only the shove. Both boys ended up outside the principal's office, and Joseph's parents were called in that afternoon.
Friday: The principal had listened to both sides, and the other boy was in trouble for the cap. But Joseph had a note home too. "I was the one being bullied," he told Nazia, "and now I'm in trouble as well." Nazia said, "Next time we go to Sir together."

qa.q: Where did the boy toss Joseph's cap?
qa.a: Onto the canteen roof.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when he said he was in trouble as well?
qa.a: Frustrated and resentful, feeling it was unfair that he was punished after being bullied.

qa.q: What else could Joseph have done on Monday?
qa.a: Taken Nazia's advice and told a teacher, so the adults dealt with the cap before it turned into a fight.

qa.q: How does Nazia see things on Friday?
qa.a: Nazia is supportive and offers to go to Sir together next time.

grounding: Over a week, a boy who pushes a bully in anger ends up in the principal's office too, learning that revenge put him in trouble.

subtype: Approach: hitting back in anger [Pitfall]
passage: Zeenat, you want to hit him back? Sit with me a minute. When I was your age, in our mohalla school, a boy two classes above took my tiffin every single day. One morning I'd had enough. I, Irfan, the smallest boy in Class 5, punched him in the stomach in front of everyone. For one second I felt like a hero. Then the headmaster came. The big boy said I'd hit him for nothing. We both had to stand outside the headmaster's room all afternoon, and my father had to leave his shop and come to school. The tiffin thief got into trouble, but so did I. What I should have done was tell my teacher in the first week, not punch him in the fourth. Now tell me what this boy has been doing. I'll ring your class teacher this evening, and tomorrow we'll go in together.

qa.q: What did the older boy take every day?
qa.a: Irfan's tiffin.

qa.q: How did young Irfan feel right after the punch?
qa.a: Like a hero for one second, then scared and in trouble when the headmaster came.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story would you change?
qa.a: Telling a teacher in the first week instead of punching in the fourth, so the adults could stop it without Irfan being punished too.

qa.q: How might Irfan's father have felt when he was called to school?
qa.a: Worried and probably disappointed, having to leave his shop because his son had hit someone.

grounding: An elder recalls hitting a bully and being punished too, and then acts that evening on the child's own report.

subtype: Approach: staying with a group of friends [Action]
passage: In their small town, Shalini noticed a pattern. The older girl who pulled her plait and called her names only did it when Shalini was alone: at the handpump behind the school, or on the lane to the bus stand. Never when her friends Sahil and Meena were with her. So Shalini made a plan. She asked Sahil and Meena to wait for her after the last bell and walk to the bus together. At break she took her tiffin to the bench under the teachers' tree instead of the handpump. She also told her class teacher, Mrs Rao, that afternoon. Mrs Rao listened, said it wasn't Shalini's fault, promised to be at the bus stand at four, and spoke to the older girl's teacher before the bell. For two weeks the lane was quiet.

qa.q: Where did the older girl bother Shalini?
qa.a: At the handpump behind the school, or on the lane to the bus stand.

qa.q: What was Shalini thinking when she noticed the pattern?
qa.a: She felt hopeful, seeing that she was only targeted when alone, and determined to plan around it.

qa.q: What else could keep Shalini safe on days her friends are absent?
qa.a: Waiting near Mrs Rao or another teacher until the bus comes, and telling Mrs Rao if anything happens.

qa.q: What is the plan like for Sahil and Meena?
qa.a: They wait after the bell and walk with Shalini, and their company keeps their friend safe.

grounding: A girl sees she is picked on only when alone, so she walks with friends and stays near teachers, and also tells her teacher.

subtype: Approach: staying with a group of friends [Action]
passage: On the way home through the park in Leicester, Nkechi realised something. The Year 6 boy who called her "Big Hair" and kicked her bag only did it when she walked alone. On days she walked with Rania, he just looked. So on Monday she asked Rania and Rania's cousin to walk the park path with her. At lunch she ate at the table nearest Ms Hollis, who was on duty. The boy hovered by the door and left. That evening Nkechi told her dad everything. He listened, told her none of it was her fault, and wrote to her teacher before dinner. Ms Hollis replied that night: she would speak to the boy and his parents in the morning.

qa.q: What did the Year 6 boy call Nkechi?
qa.a: "Big Hair".

qa.q: How did Nkechi feel when she saw the pattern?
qa.a: Hopeful and a bit relieved, understanding that the boy picked moments when she was alone.

qa.q: What else could Nkechi do if the boy starts coming near her lunch table?
qa.a: Tell Ms Hollis straight away, since the duty teacher is right there.

qa.q: What is the plan like for Rania?
qa.a: Rania walks with Nkechi and becomes part of what keeps her friend safe.

grounding: A girl notices a bully targets her only when alone, walks with friends, sits near the duty teacher and tells her father, who contacts the school.

subtype: Approach: rehearsing a calm firm reply [Thinking]
passage: In the bathroom of their flat in Seville, Alejandro faced the mirror and said, "Stop it." His voice came out squeaky. He tried again, lower. "Stop it." Better. For a week a boy in his class had been flicking his ears in the lunch queue, and Alejandro kept freezing. His mum had spoken to his teacher that afternoon, and the teacher had promised to watch the queue. But Alejandro wanted his own plan too. "If he laughs," he told himself, "I still say it, and I walk to Señora Ruiz. If he follows, I keep walking." His sister Astrid knocked. "Want me to be him?" She flicked his ear. "Stop it," Alejandro said, steady this time, and walked out of the bathroom. Astrid grinned. "That was actually scary."

qa.q: Where did Alejandro practise?
qa.a: In the bathroom of their flat, facing the mirror.

qa.q: What was Alejandro feeling as he imagined how the boy might react?
qa.a: He imagined the boy laughing and following him, thinking ahead so he would feel less shaken; nervous but determined.

qa.q: What else could Alejandro add to his plan?
qa.a: Stand near friends in the lunch queue, and tell Señora Ruiz each time it happens.

qa.q: How does Astrid see the final try?
qa.a: Astrid is impressed, saying it was actually scary.

grounding: A boy rehearses a calm, firm reply in the mirror, imagining how the bully will react, while adults already know.

subtype: Approach: rehearsing a calm firm reply [Thinking]
passage: In the counsellor's room at the government school, Manoj stood in front of the long mirror that usually hung behind the door. The counsellor, Karthik-sir, had already called Manoj's parents that morning and spoken to the Class 7 teacher about the boys who blocked Manoj on the stairs. "The adults are dealing with them," Karthik-sir said. "This is so you feel steadier in the moment." Manoj looked at himself. "Stop it," he whispered. "Again. Feet planted." "Stop it." Louder. "Now imagine they laugh. What will you do?" Manoj thought. "Say it once more and walk to the staffroom." He practised it five times, walking to the door each time. By the last one, his hands had stopped shaking.

qa.q: Where does the long mirror usually hang?
qa.a: Behind the door.

qa.q: How was Manoj feeling at the first 'Stop it'?
qa.a: Nervous, whispering, with shaking hands.

qa.q: What else could Manoj do if the boys block the stairs again?
qa.a: Walk to the staffroom as planned and tell Karthik-sir the same day.

qa.q: How might Manoj's parents feel after the morning call?
qa.a: Worried, but reassured that the school counsellor and teacher are already acting.

grounding: A boy rehearses a steady reply in front of a mirror with a counsellor, imagining the bullies' reaction, while adults handle the behaviour.

subtype: Approach: trying to become friends with the bully [Thinking]
passage: In the village school near Ajmer, a girl two classes up, Mehak, kept hiding Neelam's slate and calling her names. Neelam had told Masterji on Monday, and he had spoken to Mehak and seated her near his desk. That evening Neelam thought about Mehak. "She always eats alone. Her mother went to the city for work." Maybe she's lonely, Neelam thought. On Wednesday she passed Mehak at the handpump and said, "Your plaits are nice." Mehak looked surprised and said nothing mean that day. But on Friday the names started again at the gate. Neelam didn't try another compliment. She went straight back to Masterji, who walked her to the gate himself and said he would speak to Mehak's grandmother that evening.

qa.q: Where had Mehak's mother gone?
qa.a: To the city for work.

qa.q: What was Neelam thinking about Mehak that evening?
qa.a: She felt some sympathy, wondering whether Mehak was lonely.

qa.q: What else should Neelam keep doing alongside the kind word?
qa.a: Keep telling Masterji each time, since kindness can help but the adults must handle the behaviour.

qa.q: How might Mehak have experienced the compliment?
qa.a: Mehak looked surprised and said nothing mean that day, so it may have touched her, at least briefly.

grounding: After telling a teacher, a girl wonders if the bully is lonely and tries a kind word, which helps briefly but does not replace adult help.

subtype: Approach: trying to become friends with the bully [Thinking]
passage: At their school in Melbourne, a girl in Wei's class kept knocking her pencil case off the desk and whispering, "Nobody likes you." Wei had told Mr Abebe, her teacher, on Tuesday, and he had spoken to the girl and moved her seat that same afternoon. Still, Wei kept thinking. The girl had changed schools twice this year and never had a partner at lunch. "Maybe she's lonely, and being mean is what she knows," Wei thought. On Thursday, while they were both waiting for the bus, Wei offered her half an orange. The girl took it without a word. On Friday there was no whisper. On Monday it started again, and Wei went straight to Mr Abebe, who said he would call the girl's parents that day.

qa.q: How many times had the girl changed schools this year?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What was Wei thinking about the girl?
qa.a: Wei felt some compassion, wondering whether the girl was lonely.

qa.q: What else should Wei do if the whispers continue?
qa.a: Keep reporting to Mr Abebe each time, since a kind gesture is not a substitute for adult help.

qa.q: How does Mr Abebe respond?
qa.a: He moves the girl's seat the same afternoon, and on Monday says he will call her parents that day.

grounding: After reporting to her teacher, a girl tries kindness toward a possibly lonely bully, which helps briefly but still needs adult help.

subtype: Approach: hiding at home and skipping school [Pitfall]
passage: It was the week before exams, and Gautam had said his stomach hurt three mornings in a row. Each time his mother let him stay home, and each time, by eleven, he was fine and watching his brother Hemant's old cartoons. On Thursday she found him at the window, watching the school bus pass, shoulders hunched up to his ears. She sat beside him. "Your stomach doesn't hurt, does it?" Gautam shook his head. Then it came out: the older boys at the bus stop, the pushing, the names, the snatched lunch money. "It's not your fault," his mother said, holding his hand. "Thank you for telling me." She rang the class teacher before lunch, and the teacher met them that afternoon and put a teacher on duty at the bus stop from Friday.

qa.q: How many mornings did Gautam say his stomach hurt?
qa.a: Three mornings in a row.

qa.q: What do Gautam's hunched shoulders suggest?
qa.a: He was tense and anxious, dreading the bus stop.

qa.q: What else could Gautam have done instead of staying home?
qa.a: Told his mother or a teacher on the first day, so the adults could act before exams came close.

qa.q: How does Gautam's mother respond once he tells her?
qa.a: She listens, says it is not his fault, thanks him, calls the teacher before lunch and meets the teacher that afternoon.

grounding: A boy fakes illness to avoid bullies before exams, which brings only brief relief, until his mother notices and acts the same day.

subtype: Approach: hiding at home and skipping school [Pitfall]
passage: On the fridge calendar in their Hyderabad flat, Nitin's mother noticed something: three red crosses, all on Wednesdays. Headache, Nitin had said each time. Wednesdays were swimming days. That Wednesday morning Nitin said the headache word again, and she didn't reach for the phone to call the school. She sat on his bed instead. "Every Wednesday, Nitin. What happens on Wednesdays?" Nitin pulled the blanket up. "Mridul and his friends... in the changing room. They hide my clothes and laugh." His voice cracked. His mother held him. "You did nothing wrong. I'm glad you told me." By ten she was in the principal's office with Nitin beside her, and the principal called the swimming coach in while they were still there.

qa.q: On which day were the crosses?
qa.a: Wednesdays.

qa.q: What does Nitin pulling the blanket up suggest?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and scared to say what was happening.

qa.q: What could Nitin do if something like this starts again?
qa.a: Tell his mother or the coach the same day, instead of staying home and hoping it passes.

qa.q: What would change if Nitin's mother had simply called in sick again?
qa.a: The bullying in the changing room would have continued unseen, and Nitin would keep missing school.

grounding: A boy avoids swimming days by claiming headaches until his mother spots the pattern, asks, and takes it to the school that morning.

subtype: Approach: changing the plan when the first step fails [Revision]
passage:
"Ammi, Abbu, can I tell you something? Promise you won't get angry."
"We promise. What is it, Ayesha?"
"Karthik and his friends call me Bulldozer in class. For three weeks."
"Three weeks! Why didn't you say?"
"Because Didi said if I ignored them, they'd stop. I ignored them. They didn't stop. Today they said it in front of the whole bench."
Abbu put down his tea. "You did the right thing telling us now. This is not your fault."
Ammi was already writing in her diary. "I'm calling your class teacher tonight, and we'll meet her tomorrow."
Next evening:
"Ayesha, the teacher has moved your seat to the front row, and she'll watch that group at lunch."
"Front row?"
"Beside Sunita. And if anything happens, you tell her that same day."

qa.q: What do Karthik and his friends call Ayesha?
qa.a: Bulldozer.

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel before telling her parents?
qa.a: Anxious, asking them to promise not to get angry.

qa.q: What could the family do if the group keeps going?
qa.a: Report it again the same day and ask the teacher for a follow-up meeting, rather than going back to ignoring.

qa.q: How do Ammi and Abbu respond?
qa.a: Calmly: Abbu says it isn't her fault, and Ammi calls the teacher that night and meets the teacher the next day.

grounding: When ignoring the teasing fails, a girl tells her parents, who meet the teacher, and the school changes the seating and watches the group.

subtype: Approach: changing the plan when the first step fails [Revision]
passage: In Class 6, a boy named Harsha started calling me "Duck" because of the way I walk. I'm Nandini. My plan at first was to pretend I hadn't heard, because my cousin said bullies get bored. For about ten days I stared at my notebook and kept my face still. It didn't work. It got worse, and others joined in. One evening I told Amma and Appa everything, crying. They didn't shout. Appa said it wasn't my fault, and Amma phoned my class teacher that same night. Two days later the teacher moved Harsha to the other side of the room and kept an eye on his group at recess. The name stopped. Looking back, I'm glad I changed plans instead of waiting it out.

qa.q: What name did Harsha call Nandini?
qa.a: "Duck".

qa.q: How did Nandini feel when telling Amma and Appa?
qa.a: Nandini was upset and crying, and later glad about changing plans.

qa.q: What could Nandini do if a new name starts?
qa.a: Tell the teacher or Amma and Appa the same day, instead of waiting ten days.

qa.q: How did Amma and Appa respond?
qa.a: Calmly: Appa said it wasn't Nandini's fault, and Amma phoned the class teacher that same night.

grounding: Looking back, a child describes switching from ignoring teasing to telling parents, who contacted the teacher, and the school acted.

subtype: Approach: standing up for a friend with others [Action]
passage:
"Sumit, look. They're doing it to Dev again."
"The water bottle thing?"
"Yes. They've got it and they're making him beg."
"I can't go alone, Tanvi. There are four of them."
"Then we don't go alone. Me, you and Rehan."
"Rehan! Come."
The three of them walked over and stood beside Dev.
"Give it back," Sumit said. His voice shook. "We're all going to Miss Elizabeth."
The boys laughed, but they dropped the bottle.
Five minutes later, in the staffroom:
"Miss Elizabeth, some boys took Dev's bottle and made fun of him. It's happened before."
"Thank you for coming together. Dev, are you all right?"
"...Yes, Miss."
"I'll speak to those boys before the next bell, and I'll call Dev's parents today."

qa.q: How many boys had Dev's bottle?
qa.a: Four.

qa.q: Why wouldn't Sumit go alone, and how did he feel?
qa.a: He was scared of four boys; with friends beside him he felt brave enough, though his voice still shook.

qa.q: What else could the friends do if it happens again?
qa.a: Go to a teacher straight away, together, and stay with Dev until an adult arrives.

qa.q: What might it be like for Dev when three classmates stand beside him?
qa.a: Dev is probably relieved to be less alone, though he stays quiet and shaken.

grounding: A boy and two friends stand beside a mocked classmate and take it to a teacher, finding courage in their number.

subtype: Approach: standing up for a friend with others [Action]
passage: Last winter a new boy, Rishi, joined our class, and a few older boys started copying his stammer at the gate. I'm Pankaj. The first day I watched and did nothing, and felt sick all evening. The next day I asked Urmila and Faiz to come with me. We didn't fight. We just walked over and stood on either side of Rishi. One of the older boys said, "What do you want?" I said, "We're going to tell Sir." My knees were shaking, but with three of us it didn't feel impossible. We walked Rishi straight to our class teacher, who listened, thanked us, and took the older boys to the principal before the first period. After that, the gate was quiet. Alone I was scared, but three of us together were brave enough.

qa.q: What were the older boys copying?
qa.a: Rishi's stammer.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel after doing nothing on the first day?
qa.a: Sick all evening, probably guilty for just watching.

qa.q: What else could Pankaj have done on the first day?
qa.a: Found a teacher straight away, even alone, since telling an adult does not need a group.

qa.q: What might it be like for Rishi when three classmates stand beside him?
qa.a: Rishi would likely feel less alone and safer, especially when they walk him to the teacher.

grounding: Looking back, a child describes standing beside a mocked classmate with two friends and telling a teacher, the group giving courage.
